title: The Deal Desk, episode 28: Week four review, from the first approach to the first day of trading
hook: Kraft Heinz bid one hundred and forty-three billion dollars for Unilever and walked away two days later. Six episodes of buying and selling companies, tested the way an interviewer would. Then the owner of National Express gets a forty-six pence approach from a group backed by its largest shareholder.
voice_version: gemini-3.8-flash-tts|Sadaltager|a senior London mergers and acquisitions banker in his late thirties, presenting a finance podcast; slightly lower, deeper register than usual; measured, informative and authoritative, like an FT or Bloomberg presenter explaining to a smart listener; clear and composed, warm but never sarcastic, smug or casual|Autonoe|a curious young university student; bright and engaged, conversational|chunks-v2

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: This is The Deal Desk, episode twenty-eight. Review day. Week four was about buying and selling whole companies: synergies, the deal process, accretion and dilution, goodwill, hostile bids and the I-P-O. Today I take Sofia through all of it, no notes. If you're listening, answer before she does.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: No notes again. Fine.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: We start with one story that touches almost every episode. On Friday the seventeenth of February twenty seventeen, Unilever told the market it had received a proposal from Kraft Heinz. Fifty dollars a share: thirty dollars and twenty-three cents in cash, plus zero point two two two of a share in the combined company. An equity value of about one hundred and forty-three billion dollars, and a premium of eighteen percent to the previous day's close.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Cash and shares, like Mittal's first offer for Arcelor.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Same idea. Unilever rejected it that day. It said the proposal fundamentally undervalued Unilever, and saw no merit, financial or strategic, for its shareholders. And because the approach was now public, the British Takeover Code started a clock: Kraft Heinz had until five in the afternoon on the seventeenth of March to make a firm offer or walk away.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: A rejected approach, made public. The bear hug from episode twenty-six.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: It looked like the start of one. Unilever's shares rose about thirteen percent during the day. Then on Sunday the nineteenth, two days later, Kraft Heinz withdrew. In its words, it was best to step away early.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Why give up so fast?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Look at who owned Kraft Heinz. Berkshire Hathaway, about twenty-seven percent, and three G Capital, about twenty-four. Berkshire had written in its annual report that it would join only with partners making friendly acquisitions. A fight was off the table. So, which of this week's episodes are in this story?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Hostile bids: a public approach and a board saying no. The deal process: a deadline, and a bidder still at the approach stage. Synergies, because three G was known for cutting costs. And goodwill, because two years later Kraft Heinz wrote down fifteen point four billion dollars, including the Kraft and Oscar Mayer trademarks.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Good. And the thirteen percent? The offer was eighteen percent above the old price, and the shares only went up thirteen.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: The market thought a deal was likely, but not certain.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Right. The gap between the share price and the offer is the market's view of the risk. Keep that, because it comes back in today's deal of the day. Now the week's other stories, one line each. A-B InBev and SABMiller?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: A fifty percent premium, paid for one point four billion dollars a year of promised savings.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Twitter?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Musk tried to walk away, and the contract made him close.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: LinkedIn and Arm?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Microsoft told its shareholders the deal would dilute earnings for two years. And Arm raised nothing from its own listing, because SoftBank sold the shares.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Different stories, one question: who gets paid, and how much. Round one, synergies. Millions of euros. Cost savings of eighty a year before tax, a twenty-five percent tax rate, a ten percent discount rate, no growth. What are they worth?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Sixty after tax, over ten percent. Six hundred, before the one-off costs and the wait.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Clean. Say six hundred is the net figure. The target is worth two thousand on its own, and the buyer offers two thousand four hundred. How much of the synergies has it paid away?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Four hundred of premium out of six hundred. Two thirds. And the walk-away price is two thousand six hundred.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Round two, the process. Bidder A offers one thousand two hundred, with a financing condition and a one in five chance the money doesn't arrive. Bidder B offers one thousand, fully financed.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Eighty percent of one thousand two hundred is nine hundred and sixty. B, and that's before counting the damage of a failed sale.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Right. And after signing, can the buyer walk away by paying the reverse termination fee?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Only in the cases the contract sets out, like the debt not arriving. Otherwise the seller can ask for specific performance. Ask Musk.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Round three, accretion and dilution. Atlas earns one hundred and sixty, has one hundred and sixty million shares, and trades at sixteen euros. Earnings per share, one euro. It buys a company earning twenty, for four hundred. Twenty times. All in shares.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Twenty-five million new shares. One hundred and eighty over one hundred and eighty-five: about ninety-seven cents. Dilutive, because a price to earnings of sixteen is buying one of twenty.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Now pay with debt at six percent, tax twenty-five percent.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Interest twenty-four, eighteen after tax. One hundred and sixty-two over one hundred and sixty: about one euro and one cent. Accretive. So debt makes it the better deal.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: First trap. Same company, same price. Only the financing changed. The deal hasn't got better; the yardstick has. Debt at four and a half percent after tax looks cheap, but it adds risk that earnings per share doesn't see. Accretion tells you about the financing, not whether four hundred is the right price.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: And Microsoft was the same point the other way round.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Exactly. Round four, goodwill. Atlas pays two thousand for a company with book net assets of five hundred. Write-ups of six hundred, mostly a brand and customer relationships. Tax twenty-five percent.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Deferred tax on the write-ups, one hundred and fifty. Fair value of net assets, five hundred plus six hundred minus one hundred and fifty: nine hundred and fifty. Goodwill, one thousand and fifty.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Good. Two years later, goodwill is impaired by three hundred, not tax deductible. Cash?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Net income down three hundred. And cash down three hundred, because the value is gone.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Second trap. The value is gone; the cash went two years ago. The impairment is added back on the cash flow statement, so cash doesn't move. Goodwill falls to seven hundred and fifty, retained earnings fall by three hundred, and it balances. Kraft Heinz in miniature.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: That one's staying with me this time.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Round five, hostile bids. Unaffected price forty euros. A leak pushes the shares to forty-six. The bidder offers fifty. Premium?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Twenty-five percent, over the forty. Against forty-six it's under nine percent, which is the number the target's board would love to quote.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: And then the shares trade at fifty-two?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: The market expects a higher bid. And in Britain the board can't issue new shares to block it without shareholder approval. It argues, or finds a white knight.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Round six, the I-P-O. A company sells forty million shares at fifteen euros. Ten million are new, thirty million come from the private equity owner. What does the company raise?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Six hundred million.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Third trap. The offer raises six hundred million. The company only gets the new shares: one hundred and fifty. The other four hundred and fifty go to the seller. And if the shares close the first day at eighteen?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Three euros on forty million shares. One hundred and twenty million left on the table.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: So where did you slip?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Debt making a deal better. An impairment as cash. And who gets the money from an I-P-O.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Each time, something that looked like money was counted as money. Ask every time: whose money, and when?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: What they'll ask you. First, the question that joins the week: your client wants to buy a listed competitor. How do you decide what to offer?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Value the target with a D-C-F and comparables, add a premium of about thirty percent, and check it's accretive.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: A list of tools, not a decision. Strong answer: start with the target on its own, from the football field: comparables, precedents, a D-C-F. Add the synergies, after tax and one-off costs. Standalone value plus net synergies is the walk-away price. The offer sits well below that, but far enough above the unaffected price to win the board, or the shareholders if the board says no. Then test the financing: earnings per share, leverage, the credit rating. And the process: who else might bid, how certain your money is, and what you'll accept in the contract.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Second?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: A deal is accretive from year one, and the buyer's shares fall on the announcement. How?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: The market's wrong, or doesn't understand the deal.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Start by assuming it's right. Strong answer: accretion only compares the target's earnings with the cost of the money. Investors may think the price is too high, so the premium hands value to the seller. The new debt may make the buyer riskier, or the synergies may look doubtful. L-S-E-G fell about four point seven percent on the day its Octus talks came out, before anything was signed.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Deal of the day?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: A British company, a Spanish bidder, and an old shareholder. On Wednesday, the twenty-first of October, Mobico, the Birmingham-based owner of National Express, which also runs buses in Spain, Portugal and Morocco, confirmed a non-binding proposal of forty-six pence a share in cash. The bidder is Autobuses de León, jointly held by C-M-C Group and a fund managed by Asterion Industrial Partners.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Who is C-M-C?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Mobico's largest shareholder, with about twenty-six percent. It has been an investor since it sold Alsa, the Spanish coach operator, to the group in twenty oh five. Forty-six pence on about six hundred and fourteen million shares gives an equity value of about two hundred and eighty-two million pounds.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Two hundred and eighty-two million for National Express. That's cheap.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: That's the equity. A buyer also takes on Mobico's debt, so the business costs a good deal more than the headline. Episode eight, every week.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: And the premium?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Reports put it at about fifty-six percent over Tuesday's close. On Wednesday morning the shares rose about a third, to around thirty-nine and a half pence.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: So against today's price, the premium is only about sixteen percent.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Round five again. Thirty-nine and a half is a price that already contains the bid. The premium is measured against the unaffected price. And Mobico says its statement was prompted by recent movement in its share price, so check the days before Tuesday too, in case the leak started earlier.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: And the gap between thirty-nine and a half and forty-six is the market doubting the deal. Like Unilever.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Exactly the cold open. The proposal is non-binding. Autobuses de León is doing confirmatory due diligence, and under the Takeover Code it has until five in the afternoon on the eighteenth of November to make a firm offer or walk away. The same kind of clock Kraft Heinz faced.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: But this time the board likes it.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: The independent directors, which means the whole board except Jorge Cosmen, say they're minded to recommend forty-six pence if a firm offer comes on those terms. Friendly, then. But not a deal yet. Here's your interview question. The bidder is backed by a shareholder that already owns about a quarter of the company. What does that change?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: It's halfway there already.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: A head start, not halfway. Strong answer: the bidder's side starts with about a quarter of the shares, which makes life hard for a rival, like the irrevocable at Steyr. It also knows the business better than any outsider, so the other shareholders should ask whether forty-six pence reflects what it knows. That's why only the independent directors give a view, and why they have to test the price against the football field, not just against Tuesday's close.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Quiz. For you listening. Question one: cost savings of eighty a year before tax, a twenty-five percent tax rate, a ten percent discount rate and no growth. What are they worth? Question two: a buyer on sixteen times earnings buys a target at twenty times, at the offer price, all in shares, with no synergies. Accretive or dilutive? Question three: a buyer pays two thousand for net assets with a book value of five hundred, write-ups of six hundred and a twenty-five percent tax rate. How much goodwill? Question four: an I-P-O sells forty million shares at fifteen euros, ten million of them new. How much does the company receive? Question five: Mobico's shares rose to around thirty-nine and a half pence, against a proposal of forty-six. What is the gap telling you?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Pause here if you want to think it through.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Answers. One: six hundred. Sixty after tax, over ten percent. Two: dilutive. The target's earnings yield, five percent, is below the cost of the buyer's shares, about six and a quarter. Three: one thousand and fifty. Five hundred, plus six hundred, minus one hundred and fifty of deferred tax, is nine hundred and fifty of fair value. Four: one hundred and fifty million euros; the other four hundred and fifty goes to the seller. Five: the market isn't sure a firm offer will come at forty-six pence.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Four weeks ago I thought the price was the deal. Now it's where the argument starts.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: And next week, the argument is about debt. Tomorrow, episode twenty-nine: what a leveraged buyout is, and the fight for R-J-R Nabisco, the biggest leveraged buyout of its time.
